utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the card and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, could we have your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that your date of birth is the 15th of October, 1945; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That your ethnicity is Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that you are currently retired?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, please, with your background. Is it right that you completed the JNA school for non-commissioned officers, and you were then subsequently enrolled at the military academy. You graduated in 1969 as an infantry officer, and then in 1982 you graduated from the command staff academy? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your active military service runs from 1963 until 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That during your military career you commanded all units from platoon to brigade level; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Prior to taking over command of the 80th Motorised Brigade in September 1991, is it right you had been the commander of the 11th Partisan Brigade in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the 80th Motorised Brigade, is it correct that you held the post of being in command until the 30th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In 1995 until your subsequent retirement in 2002, is it correct that you performed duties relating to training at the headquarters of the 12th Corps at Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, up to 2001 only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is a misprint in the document. And can I just deal with your overall grading by your commanders. Is it right that the classification, I believe, is from 1 till 5, that 1 is, I presume, poor, and 5 is the other end, towards excellence. What were your gradings, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part 4 and 5, very good and excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you have given evidence in relation to principally this matter on no less than I think it is five occasions. You were interviewed at Belgrade on the 12th of January, 1998, again interviewed in Belgrade on the --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There were hearings at Belgrade, I think 24th and 25th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And an interview at Belgrade, slightly out of sequence, the 21st of November, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And may I conclude with regard to your testimonies or statements made, is it right that you made a statement for OTP here on the 25th, 26th of September, 2003, concluding on the 2nd of October, 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to deal at the very start of your evidence. Again with my learned friends' leave, I will lead the early part and try to avoid any contentious matters. Is it right that on the 29th of October, 1991, the 80th Motorised Brigade began deploying temporarily in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That the deployment of your brigade was completed around the 7th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And from its arrival until its departure -- sorry, from its arrival until the departure of the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade, the 80th was subordinated to OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can you, from your own independent recollection, remember when it was the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think, as far as I can recall, it left Vukovar on the 25th or the 26th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to deal with what I will call TO units. Is it right that you had TO units from Serbia included -- or should I say were subordinated to you at that time? So it's TO units from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were any of the TO units from Eastern Slavonia subordinated to your brigade and whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have any volunteer units that were subordinated to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, did you notice line 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do now. I'll ask the question again, although I think it's a fairly straightforward answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, I want to ask a question again. Sometimes there is an electrical fault that causes problems for the translation. I'll ask the following question again: Were any of the TO units from Eastern Slavonia subordinated to your brigade whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I just deal with your period of service, and I will come back to it at the end of your evidence, I hope. Can you tell us when it was that the 80th Motorised Brigade left Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And after the departure of the 80th Motorised Brigade, did you remain in the area or did you leave with them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade and its units returned in their entirety, but some of the officers in the brigade command remained in town. I returned, but I cannot recall when I went to Kragujevac, some eight or ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So, that's, as you believe it, eight or ten days after the 14th of January - is that right - but you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, there seems to be another problem with the interpretation. I'm wondering whether the microphone is operating properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please wait for the witness to reply before putting the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I think it's right to say that you believe that eight or ten days after the 14th of January, that's when you left the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, then, please with your arrival in Eastern Slavonia at the end of October. Did you know any of the officers of OG South when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: First let me say that I didn't arrive in late October with my unit -- with all my units, there was only one battalion. I came with the other units on the 7th of November, and at that time I didn't know any of the officers from the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of OG South upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the OG was Colonel Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to your dealings with him, were there any briefings that you were obliged to attend?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: There were regular briefings in the command in Negoslavci where Colonel Mile Mrksic was. I can't recall precisely, but from the 7th or 8th I attended regularly until they withdrew and went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever see Major General Zivota Panic at any of those daily briefings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Arkan at any of those meetings of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the security of the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade and OG South at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was Major Veselin Sljivancanin; he was a major at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 6, line 5, when the witness was referring to these regular briefings, he said that they were held between the -- between 1700 and 1800 hours, but this did not enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We also have an ability to understand. I wonder if that could be listened to by the interpreter because there was no interruption by me. But I will ask in any event, and I had not asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, the briefings themselves, did you mention any time when those briefings were to be held in reply to the question that I posed earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think they were held from 1800 or 1900 hours. I don't recall the precise time when they started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal then, please, with Major Sljivancanin. You said he was in charge of the security of the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade and OG South. Did he have any other duty in connection with your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that now, except that he was the chief of Operative Group South and he probably cooperated with my security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me, there seems to be another problem with translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When -- would Your Honour forgive me while I just check what has been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have said that he was chief of security. Can we deal, please, with who was your security officer at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: My security officer at that time was reserve Captain First Class Dragi Vukosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know if he had any contact with Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but through the chain of the security, I think he should have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say the "chain of security," do you mean the chain of the command security? Can you explain, please, what you mean by "chain of the security."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the chain of command within the security. The senior security organ was Major Sljivancanin, and all the security organs in the subordinate units were, in a manner, subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with your brigade. Did it have any police -- military police attachments or units at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what unit it was.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was a military police company with one military police platoon and one traffic platoon. They were within our composition all that time. One military police platoon was subordinated to another unit throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In the British army a platoon is normally about 30 or 32 bodies. What is the numbering for a platoon normally within the JNA in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the formation, 25 to 30 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then with the strength, please, the actual strength of your military police company and the platoons that you have referred to. You have told us there was one military police platoon and one traffic platoon. What were the actual numbering, if you are able to remember, of the military police platoon existing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think at that time a military police platoon, that one had about 25 men; but some of them were always absent for various reasons, either on sick leave or for other reasons, whereas the traffic platoon had two squads of 15 to 16 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is each squad then 15 to 16 men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The military police squad was a little bigger than the traffic squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, how big was one traffic platoon -- sorry, one traffic squad or squad contained within a traffic --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were 15 or 16 men. One squad had seven men and the eighth was the leader, and a similar situation obtained in the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So in reality, the traffic platoon has somewhere between 15 and 16 men in total; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The military police, who gave them orders?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Usually it was the chief of security who issued orders to the military police, as did the Chief of Staff. Perhaps some of the operative organs if the people I mentioned previously were absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about security organs? Did they or were they able to give orders to the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially in professional matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that none of the units that you had were directly involved in combat operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if it's not right can you tell us then, please, exactly what the situation was at that time, vis-a-vis combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not one of my units in the military police company participated in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was your task then at that time when you were based in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived on the 7th of November with my unit and when I established the brigade units, I was deployed for the most part in the area of the town of Vukovar, the broader area of the town. In Negoslavci, Sremske Laze, the 1st Battalion at that time was within OG North across the River Vuka. And all the other units were south of Vukovar. The 3rd Battalion was at the entrance to Vukovar, that's where it was deployed. And for the most part their task was to take up positions there, to organise themselves. As they were all reservists, they did not participate in the combat operations which were already going on in the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Obviously the word "brigade" suggests a large military unit, but the actuality can often be different. May we deal, please, with the battalions that you had at that time, the infantry battalions. Were they subordinated to OG South or not at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: They were subordinated to OG South, almost all of them were. I can't remember whether it was the 3rd Battalion and the artillery unit and the anti-aircraft unit which were resubordinated. Part of the military police company remained in my troops, as did the logistics battalion, the staff command, the communications company. The other units were later resubordinated to Operative Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we were trying to explain this to civilians and they asked the question of you: As of mid-November, what unit were actually subordinated to you, Colonel Vojnovic? What was the actual strength of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the brigade command, the staff brigade, the communications company, the reconnaissance company, part of the military police company, the rear battalion - and I'm not sure about the 3rd Battalion, I don't think that was there - but these were all units which did not have the full manpower levels, according to the establishment. The manpower levels were only 50 to 60 per cent of the establishment levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about the anti-aircraft defence light artillery battalion? We know it as the LAD PVO.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The LAD PVO was subordinated to OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Right. May I deal then, please, with what I will call the Vukovar TO or local Serbian forces. You have told us that you had no local Serbian forces subordinated to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But is it equally correct to say that you did meet some of their leaders or commanders during your period of tour in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't meet them, and I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, when you say you "didn't meet them," if we deal with situations generally, did you ever meet or see a man called Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw Stanko Vujanovic was at Ovcara, on the 20th of November. Like all the other members of the TO who I saw at the time, up to that time I did not see them or know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever see or meet Miroljub Vojnovic while you were in Vukovar -- Vujovic. Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I also saw Miroljub Vujovic for the first time at Ovcara on the 20th of November, just like Stanko Vujanovic and the other members of the TO who were there at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will return to that in due course, but I would like to deal, please, with what I will call evacuations. Did your brigade ever become responsible for the evacuation of any groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: My brigade was responsible for evacuations only of a single group of civilians, women and children. There were seven or eight buses which, before the events in Ovcara, had been in the Ovcara area. They arrived in these buses, we secured them all, and transported them in an organised manner to certain locations we had been told to take them to. This was a large group of civilians, including women, children and elderly men whom we secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I will deal with the timing of that in a moment. But were you ever aware of an evacuation of prisoners from Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We secured the prisoners from Mitnica at the Ovcara hangar the whole night, and this was a task given to me -- by me to my officers. I wasn't sure about the soldiers, because a number of the soldiers were the reserves, so I engaged the most responsible senior officers from the brigade, starting with the Chief of Staff, the security organ, and other senior officers from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what I want to do is just to clarify the sequence, and then I will return to Mitnica. Can you remember whether the evacuation of the women and children was before or after the Mitnica evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I can say, and I think that this was before the evacuation of the group from Mitnica. I can't remember whether it was this group or the Mitnica group, which day it was. But I think it was on the day before, on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us then deal, please, with your role on the Mitnica evacuation. So what role did you actually have in that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: After security in the Ovcara hangar sector, our task was to transport them and evacuate them in an organised way to the Sremska Mitrovica garrison. We did that in an organised manner without a single problem. The assignment was executed and members of the brigade, and the military police handed over the said prisoners in the Sremska Mitrovica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with the arrival of the Mitnica evacuation before we deal with the departure. Now, had you any dealings with the arrival or the transportation of those evacuees coming to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We were not involved in the evacuation of the people to Ovcara. We evacuated them from Ovcara to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you had no dealings with the evacuation of the people to Ovcara. Were you there when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In very brief order, can you please tell us your first dealing with the Mitnica evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't evacuate the people from Mitnica to the hangar area. Once they were at the hangar -- I don't know exactly, I can't remember who issued the assignment for us to secure the group. That's what we did. I personally was at the hangar at the time. I saw that there were about 120 or 130 people. I know that the commander of that group was Filip Karaula, and I saw him too. And those soldiers, according to the list, were transported and regularly handed over to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was the name of the -- or can you remember the names of officers who were present at that time at Ovcara and involved in the supervision of the Mitnica group?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You mean my officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's start with your officers and then we can move on to other officers, if there are any.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: From my brigade the Mitnica group prisoners were secured by the chief of the staff, chief of security, chief of the engineers, chief of the ABHO, and some other officers which, at this moment, I cannot remember by name individually. But I know that they were guarding the Mitnica prisoners in the Ovcara sector. At the time when I was there, I didn't see other officers from other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know if Vezmarovic was involved at the Mitnica/Ovcara detention?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As commander of a company, I think Vezmarovic was involved there, and he was responsible for the transport of the prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say that you cannot remember if officers from other units were there, is it a case that you cannot remember names or you cannot remember whether actual individuals were there from other units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Right now I couldn't categorically state who was there, but I know for a fact that they were brought by other organs and officers to the Ovcara hangar sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know if Karanfilov was there or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is a leading question. On page 14, line 21 - 25, the witness replied about his knowledge and that he didn't see other officers there and in line 25. So in this way it's being suggested to the witness to give an answer which he has already given. According to him, it's not even known who that man was. But as for this particular topic, I think that an answer was already given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I rely on the answer given by the witness at 15:6 and 7, where the witness says that they were brought by other organs and officers. And I said was he there or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the task of identifying whether or not certain critical players, if I can use that phrase, were present, is one of importance in this exercise. Mr. Moore has asked in general terms and then has sought specifically: This name, was he there or not? This name, there or not? I think in the circumstances that is an appropriate way, and if you want to make something in cross-examination of the change between a general answer that didn't include a particular witness and then an answer, if one comes, that he did know a particular witness, it's open to you. Please carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. You said you saw other organs and officers. I asked the question: "Do you know if Karanfilov was there or not?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Karanfilov at that time, so I really couldn't say whether he was there at that time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the date that the Mitnica evacuation arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Or do my learned friends object if I would lead with that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was the 19th of November when the Mitnica group was brought to the hangar section. According to what I saw, according to my knowledge, it was approximately at 10.00, but I really don't have the exact time. Nobody was really paying attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was going to correct the witness to the proper date with the Court's leave, and as long as there's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, the Mitnica evacuation actually arrived on the 18th of November and departed on the 19th. It's just a -- so that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that we saw the group off on the 19th or, rather, evacuated it to Sremska Mitrovica. I don't know the exact date -- or I didn't say the exact date when it got there. I think that it came on the same day that it was evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, we know that it came on the 18th and we know that it departed on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that on the 19th we evacuated it and guarded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to the procedure itself for Mitnica, were there any problems that you became aware of when they were under the control of Vezmarovic and his military police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: While Vezmarovic, the military police, and my officers were securing the Mitnica group there were no problems. They were transported in an organised manner in the proper way, and handed over in Sremska Mitrovica. And Vezmarovic informed about that on his return from Sremska Mitrovica, he said that there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to evacuation, you have had the one that you have referred to dealing with women and children, and you have told us now about the Mitnica evacuation. Did you report to your superior in OG South, namely Colonel Mrksic, that the evacuations had concluded?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this was done and reported on, especially in the evening meetings - there wasn't too much discussion about that - and I think that the military police, as well as the security organ did that, informed their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why would it be necessary for you to tell Colonel Mrksic about evacuations concluding?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Because we were given that assignment, and when we carried out the assignment, it is regular military procedure to report that the assignment was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who gave you those assignments?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly who specifically assigned this task to me, but I can assume that it was some of my superiors. Whether it was Colonel Mrksic or Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, I really cannot remember that right this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I would like to deal, please, with an evacuation that is now known as the hospital evacuation, which ended up in the Ovcara hangar. So I wish to deal with that evacuation. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you ever informed that there was another group of evacuees coming from the -- in this case the hospital, and where you were to be directly involved?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: My brigade command first didn't have any information and did not participate in the planning or organising or the execution or carrying out of the -- or bringing out the prisoners from the hospital and bringing them to the Ovcara sector. This whole process was something that happened somewhere outside of our brigade. We didn't guard the prisoners, we were not at the hospital, we didn't participate in organising them or transporting them to the Ovcara hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that another way of saying no?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not in any way participate in bringing out from the hospital of the prisoners and bringing the prisoners to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of what I will call the Vukovar Hospital evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Quite by accident. On my way back from one of my units in the Sotin sector where one of our rear battalions was located and I went to visit the battalion, I wanted on the way back to stop by at Ovcara and to see the commander of the LAD PVO battery, (redacted) who was deploying his command post in the Ovcara sector. And on the way back I saw a group, first several buses, who were standing in front of Ovcara and people who were coming out of the buses through a gauntlet. These people were beaten, they were hit, they were cursed at and they were being treated quite improperly. Some of them had their documents confiscated from them or other items. I was surprised with this situation. I didn't stop to see (redacted), who was waiting for me there, but I immediately went in front of the hangar. And with these two of my soldiers who were with me in the car, I started to defend the prisoners who were entering the hangar. And while I was doing it, I had no idea where they were coming from and who was bringing them there. I myself was harassed, pushed, hit, and there were shouts that these are not your prisoners, these are not -- these are our prisoners. I was insulted, they were saying, "What are you doing here, old man? What do you want? These are our prisoners." I myself was pushed, and as much as I was able to I prevented these people from being beaten. At that point in time (redacted) came, he was there, and he helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Clearly there will be redactions in that account, but I would like to deal with this account and break it into parts, if I may. I have some questions. You said that you saw people coming out of the bus and going through a gauntlet. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is that there was no other way for them to pass, to evade the gauntlet, because the gauntlet was formed from the door of -- the exit door of the bus to the entry door to the hangar. And they were passing through it, and that's where they were hit, kicked, insulted, humiliated, until they reached the hangar entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what were they being hit with?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: They kicked them, punched them, using their weapons first of all - I'm thinking of rifle-butts - whoever had a rifle or anything else that they had on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the people who were doing the hitting, do you know if any of them were wearing uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: They wore different clothing. Some wore uniforms, some had mixed pieces of uniform or civilian clothes. Nobody was dressed according to regulations. They were mostly wearing uniforms, but they were not completely in compliance with regulation uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to say what units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell. I was seeing these people for the first time. Are you talking about the prisoners or are you talking about these members who were beating them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, the people who were doing the attacks, the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met those people for the first time. I didn't know any of them, they were standing there as I described, in uniforms, and they were beating them as they were going through the gauntlet. I didn't know anyone. I was trying to prevent them from doing that, asked them to stop, to start behaving properly, to stop beating them. But mostly they paid no attention to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to -- the English word is "ascertain." Were you able to find out where the people who were being beaten had come from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning I didn't know when I saw all those people with (redacted) who came with two other soldiers who help me. So when all of those people entered the hangar, that was when I saw Major Vukasinovic who was standing somewhere in the middle of the hangar, close to where you entered the hangar. I was surprised to see him there. I went up to him, though, and I asked him, "Where are these people from that are being brought in?" And he answered, "From the hospital." That's when I found out that they were from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just going to delay for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. There is no need to show that courtesy. I've got two ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say that you saw Major Vukasinovic who was standing somewhere in the middle of the hangar. You say you were surprised to see him there. Firstly, who was he? What was his role?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Major Vukasinovic was the deputy chief of security in the guards brigade or, rather, in the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why were you surprised to see him in the Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I was surprised because nobody was doing anything. While the prisoners were being brought into the hangar they were being beaten, nobody was preventing this, but he was there. That's what surprised me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You asked him, "Where are these people from?" And he answered, "From the hospital."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Had you been aware of an evacuation from the hospital or that an evacuation from the hospital was to occur that morning or day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that Vukasinovic was standing somewhere in the middle. Did you see any other officers, or what I will call regular soldiers, with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a group around Vukasinovic, they were wearing regulation uniforms. They were military personnel. I don't know who they were, but mostly they were all without caps and I didn't know those people. They were all wearing our M-77 military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you just assist us what the M-77 military uniform looks like, without going into a fashion statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That was the standard uniform at the time in the Yugoslav People's Army and was olive-drab shirt and pants. There were boots and at the time we -- it was a cap that we called the Tito cap, as well as a wind-jacket. This is what all the senior officers wore, and these particular officers were wearing all of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether there were other officers present at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I could not say definitely that there were other officers. I didn't know any of them, but I did know Major Vukasinovic. I knew him and only him, and he was there. Maybe some people, some other people were there, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Lieutenant-Colonel Panic there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Lieutenant-Colonel Panic there at that time, but later I heard from conversation -- from a conversation with him, and during his testimony in Belgrade too, that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just move forward in time many years. You have described having a conversation with Panic, and I exclude the evidence that he gave. When did you have a conversation with Panic where he indicated to you that he had actually been at Ovcara but you hadn't seen him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this was during the testimony at the military court in Belgrade when we just happened to meet. He didn't know and I didn't know that we would both testify there, and that's where I heard these things from him. The fact that he was there is something that was confirmed to me by (redacted), and he was surprised that I didn't see Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, because I was in charge of taking care of the prisoners of war. So I really didn't know who was in the hangar, to the left in the hangar, to the right in the hangar and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to come back in time again to the Ovcara hangar where you are seeing Vukasinovic. Now, you have told us that he was there with, I will call, soldiers in the M-77 uniform. Did you see any of those soldiers or Vukasinovic attempt to stop the beatings that were occurring?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't like to interrupt my learned friend, and I'm sure he doesn't like it either, but I have to say that he said that Vukasinovic was with the soldiers. Because in answer to the Prosecutor's question about officers, he explained that the persons with Vukasinovic were officers. I would like there to be no misleading of the witness with such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, there is an issue about soldiers and officers. I leave it to you to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The phrase I have, I'm just looking at it very quickly is: "I saw a group around Vukasinovic, they were wearing regulation uniform. They were military personnel." That is at 22 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That doesn't answer it one way or another. In about line 23:1 you will see something perhaps a bit more to Mr. Lukic's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Soldiers, perhaps, covers -- well, it does cover officers and ordinary troops. The people that you saw with Vukasinovic, were you able to ascertain if they were officers or soldiers? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know whether they were privates or officers. All I saw was that they were neatly dressed, that they were clean-shaven with proper uniforms. But for the most part they did not have caps on, neither did Vukasinovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I remained there about half an hour, until all the prisoners had entered the hangar. As I said, I was there with Vukasinovic, I exchanged a few more words with him. I observed the situation in the hangar, and after that I got ready to leave for my command and for the briefing in the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And before we get you to actually leave, throughout that period were you able to see if there were any -- or there was a group of people outside the hangar at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the hangar at Ovcara there were some members of the Territorial Defence going in and out, milling around. I didn't really watch that very carefully. I didn't know them but, yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how would you describe the atmosphere within the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In the hangar it was quite a shocking sight. There was a lot of tension. The people were put on the left-hand side where there was some hay. People were sitting down. They were worried, anxious, looking to see what was happening. The atmosphere was not a very pleasant one, especially not for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you leave the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I left the hangar because I wanted to ask for assistance and security from my brigade command. They arrived headed by reserve Captain Svetolik [phoen] Vukic. He arrived with 15 to 20 men. There was no military police. Perhaps some of them did have military police belts on, but they were not actually the military police because Vezmarovic at that time was still in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how did Vukic know to come to the Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as we saw that the situation was complex, I acted in the way an officer should, I think. I informed someone in the brigade command - I don't know how - but that a team should be sent to help resolve the situation at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's because you're trying to give answers very quickly, but you had not told us about leaving to Ovcara and where you went to. So let's return to that. You say that you left Ovcara. Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: By your leave, let me first explain about Vukic. After a certain time - I can't tell you how long - Vukic arrived and addressed me. I grabbed him by the sleeve and pointed, saying, "Do you see that tall major? That's Major Vukasinovic." He said, "Yes, I can see him." I said, "Report to him. If you are to be given a task or if he needs some assistance in connection with the situation, ask him." I showed Vukic that, and then I left for the command post in Negoslavci, where the command of OG South was. The meeting had already started some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that I want to return to, please, is: How was it that Vukic arrived at Ovcara? Did you order him or do you know who ordered him or the reason that he arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I asked for assistance to protect the prisoners. Who transmitted this to him. Whether it was Dragi Vukosavljevic or someone else, I don't know, but I asked for help to be sent to protect the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say that you asked for help to be sent, where were you when you asked for the help to be sent? Were you still at Ovcara, or were you back in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think I was still at Ovcara, because I instructed him to go to Major Vukasinovic and ask him whether he had any tasks for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know what occurred between the conversation between Vukasinovic and Vukic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Later on I learned from Vukic on the following day, or one or two days later, that as he explained very confidently and as he testified before the special court in Belgrade, he said, "Comrade Major, I'm from the 80th Brigade. I was sent here to help you. Do you have any tasks for me?" Vukasinovic replied, "We don't have any tasks for you." Vukic went back to the entrance of the hangar. He even says that he spoke to some of the prisoners and that they even had a cigarette together. One of the prisoners was concerned and asked him what would happen to them. Vukic said to him, "Probably, the same thing will happen that happened to the group from Mitnica. You will be taken to Sremska Mitrovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I deal then, please, with your return to Negoslavci. Now, you told us that you wanted to go back and ask for assistance. Assistance from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think my learned friend may be confused. The witness didn't say he went to Negoslavci to ask for assistance. He asked for assistance from Ovcara, and he went to Negoslavci for a regular briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The reference that I have is that: I wanted to ask for assistance. Perhaps if I have jumped too far ahead, and I can't remember if I have, then I apologise. But certainly I have got this in my own handwriting and written it down as a hook to move on to other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It better be clarified I think, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly. Could I just check for a moment, if I may, on the transcript, because I know it's further back? Would Your Honour forgive me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In your reply at 27:1 you say, "I asked for assistance to protect the prisoners." And then it refers to other references. Can we just clarify to this extent: Did you ever leave Ovcara and return to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I left Ovcara when Vukic arrived with the men, and I went to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of going to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I had to go -- not I had to, but I was supposed to go the regular briefing. But I couldn't abandon the prisoners in such a situation, and for this reason I was late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with the briefing itself. When you got to the briefing, do you know what time it was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You mean at the command post in Negoslavci at Mrksic's place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you said that you had to go -- you were supposed to go to the regular briefing.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I want to deal with that. Now, where was the regular briefing held?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The briefing was held in Negoslavci in the command post of OG South. It was a regular briefing held on a daily basis at 1800 or 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you any idea what time you actually arrived? You said, I think -- that you were late for the briefing. Are you able to assess what time you actually arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that I was late for the briefing because of the complex situation at Ovcara. I think it may have been around 1900 hours, but I can't tell you the precise time to the minute I entered the room. I apologised to the commander for being late, and I explained to him the reason for my late arrival at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say you explained to him the reason for your late arrival, can you please tell the Court what it was that you said that had caused you to be late?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I said the following: "I'm coming from Ovcara. At Ovcara there's a mess. Some prisoners of war have been brought there from a hospital, I don't know. I don't know who exactly organised them and brought them there. I saw that they were being treated improperly, that they are being made to go through a gauntlet, that they were beaten with equipment people had. And I saw a man hit one of the prisoners with a rifle-butt as he was passing through the gauntlet up to the entrance to the hangar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you said that you told, the commander. Was the commander whom you told?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The commander at the time was Colonel Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you told Mrksic about this mistreatment and behaviour at Ovcara, did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When I gave him this explanation and described the situation at Ovcara, he simply waved his hand like this and said, "Don't talk to me about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you show us, please, what you mean that he "waved his hand like this." Can you demonstrate to the Court the way he treated you and waved at you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Almost all of them were there in that room, and when I reported, he said, "Don't talk to me about this." Making this gesture. I was surprised. I understood from this that he was aware of the situation, so I didn't speak about it further in that room at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we normally take a break, I think, one and a half hours. I would like to move on to another topic. It is obviously related to this, but it is a natural break point. And if Your Honour is considering rising within the next two or three minutes, I, for my part, would prefer to stop at this edge of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think there may have to be, unfortunately, some redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There will be many, and we will break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, you've told us about informing, as he was then, Colonel Mrksic. You have described the -- and shown us the gesture he made. And you told us that you didn't speak about it further in that room at the time because you understood from that he was aware of the situation. And how many people were in the room at the time he spoke to you and then demonstrated to you with his hand?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that at that point there were about 20 to 25 people in the room. These were officers from the OG South command, and also there were some other people present. I didn't count who was there, but regularly the meetings or the briefings would be attended by 20 to 25 officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did the meeting come to an end?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And we went outside in front of the room where the meeting was held. Then too I spoke with Colonel Mrksic about the situation, what happened, what I saw. And perhaps I described it a little bit more in detail than when I talked about it when I entered the room for the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you spoke to Colonel Mrksic about this on this -- what I will call this second occasion, was there anybody else present at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: First let me say yes, but before I wanted to say I didn't respond to the question. Before I left for Negoslavci you asked me, I called Dragi Vukosavljevic and sent him to go again to Ovcara to look at what the situation was, to help if anything could be done in terms of the situation that was there. That's what I wanted to say. The next thing is what you asked me about my conversation with Colonel Mrksic outside of the room where the meeting was held. Well, during the conversation Dragi Vukosavljevic came up to me. He informed me that the situation was complex, that it was hard to define, that it was serious, that members of our military police who were still there were being pushed back and could not play any significant role in the protection of the prisoners because of the attitude of the territorials, that they had in relation in them. And then at one point there was a mutual scuffling or pushing between the territorials and my unit or rather the soldiers of the military police unit of Vezmarovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with this meeting. You have told us that you were speaking to Mrksic here a second time and Vukosavljevic came up to you. When he was --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When he was explaining this situation to you, was Mrksic still present?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Mrksic was there outside -- outside when he was explaining that to me. I don't know if he heard that or not. And Dragi Vukosavljevic insisted that he also goes with me and that we once again inform Colonel Mrksic about the situation at Ovcara, which is what we did. Together I introduced Dragi Vukosavljevic to Colonel Mrksic as a good officer, a reserve senior officer from the security organ. That's what I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Here is Vukosavljevic insisting, as you say, that he goes and informs Mrksic. Now, when Vukosavljevic informed Mrksic about that, what was Mrksic's reaction, if any at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really say exactly what Mrksic told Vukosavljevic. I do know that there was a conversation, I was standing in the vicinity, but I didn't hear it. And I think that later Dragi told me that he was surprised when he saw Mrksic tell him, "Well, just leave it. Don't bother me with that kind of thing," and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any indication by Mrksic of him being aware or unaware that the 80th Motorised Brigade were at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he didn't know that we were at Ovcara, especially during the initial period. Perhaps later, through the command line he was informed about it, Panic saw me there, so this is normal. But judging by his reaction when we spoke about that situation when he told me what he did, he decisively said to me, "What were you doing there?" He told me that as the brigade commander. And I saw and understand that I really should not have been there. I didn't receive any kind of task. I didn't participate in the planning of that operation. We didn't have any assignments in relation to that assignment, so there was no other need to think about it in any other way. So simply, after that answer I understood it as an order that I shouldn't be there, and that's when I said to Dragi Vukosavljevic to come -- to go to Ovcara, to go and see Vezmarovic there, to see what the situation was, and -- I don't know what the situation was, but to stop exposing our soldiers to the danger in view of the fact that they were threatened there and that they should withdraw to the barracks. And this is what Dragi did, he went there and he did what he was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you that evening speak either to Vezmarovic or Vukosavljevic about what had happened at Ovcara after you had left?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that we spoke briefly. Vezmarovic informed me that he had already got the units ready to move, had them all packed, and that Major Karanfilov came and told him that the Territorial Defence -- actually, that the prisoners should be handed over to the jurisdiction of the Territorial Defence, in view of the fact that some government -- I guess the government of Krajina was informed of that and that the military police had no longer anything to do with that and could withdraw to the barracks, which I can say Vezmarovic agreed to with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to go into private session, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is the evening of the 20th. Are you able to inform the Court whether or not the fact that atrocities had occurred at Ovcara had become public or was known to others?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a fact. We heard it the next day. Mostly in Negoslavci the citizens of Negoslavci had already started to talk. I don't know if any of them were there or not, but in any case, there was talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you not inform -- or perhaps I am jumping the gun. Did you ever inform Mrksic about hearing that atrocities had occurred at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't inform him, I thought that he knew about that, that he was aware of that, because his most responsible senior officers were participating in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we deal from the 21st to the time that the Guards Motorised Brigade leave Vukovar, are you aware, or did you ever hear that there were a start of investigations into these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I heard at a meeting of Colonel Mrksic, this was after that, that investigative organs would come from Belgrade who would investigate this case. I didn't see him, but I know that this was something that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: At a meeting in the evening, I think, but I'm not sure if it was on the 21st or the 22nd. It was sometime during either one of those days, I can't remember exactly which day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you talk about investigations into these atrocities, was it these atrocities at Ovcara or atrocities generally?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think that this primarily referred to Ovcara. Generally there were some minor such cases, perhaps it was general. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, is it a case you know or a case you are assuming?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he told us that investigative organs would arrive in Negoslavci. I thought it was because of that. Whether it was broader than that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then, please, with the hand-over from the Guards Motorised Brigade to the 80th. Now, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think the hand-over occurred immediately before their return to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what capacity or function did you operate in when they had left?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We were then in command of the town of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was your job, what was your function at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, the tasks we had to do was to clear up the battle-field, de-mine the streets, collect carcasses of animals in the street, create the conditions for a more normal life, prevent looting by individuals, prevent people entering other people's houses and taking furniture and equipment, providing security for the people residing in the area, because there were still many individuals who had weapons who behaved in an arrogant manner. Not infrequently one would hear shooting around town and in the vicinity of the town for no special reason. We tried to do our best to provide water for the citizens, to open soup kitchens where people could come to eat. We tried to do whatever we could for the benefit of the citizens, and that's how we behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with an issue in relation to what I will call civilian leadership. As far as you're aware, was there any civilian leadership existing immediately after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the fall of Vukovar I think there was no civilian leadership. We would have had to cooperate with them had there been any, but there was actually a vacuum. And it was up to the command of the brigade to look after providing food for citizens and so on. The civilian leadership was in Vukovar, it was set up in Vukovar in December, very soon. I know that there was a meeting in Velepromet and that it was chaired by Rajko Bibic, one of the most prominent people there. He had been the managing director of the Ovcara farm. I was there as an officer to make sure there was order, to make sure that the meeting was held in an orderly manner. They elected 12 or 14 people, and this group was headed by Rajko Bibic. Some portfolio -- portfolios were distributed among them, one took charge of one area, another of another. And that's when matters began to develop in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you were operating in your capacity as town commander, who did you receive your orders from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: While I was commander of the town, mostly I received orders from the 1st Military District, of course when the guards brigade returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time receive orders or instructions from the SAO SBZS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Goran Hadzic ever visit you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to return to your dealings with the local Serbian or Vukovar TO. You told us that you had seen Milorad Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic on the 20th of November at Ovcara. What were they doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first time I had seen them at Ovcara, just like all the other territorials were there. And the impression they left on me was as if they were in charge there, as if they were in command in that place. I concluded this by the way they moved, the way they acted, the way they communicated with other members of the Territorial Defence. From all this I concluded that they were the leaders there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal with the period before the departure of the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade. Did you ever have any meetings where Major Sljivancanin was present?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was there once immediately before the return of the guards brigade to Belgrade; this was in Velepromet. I don't know how I happened to be there, but probably somebody told me. I wouldn't have gone there of my own accord if I hadn't been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, what the meeting involved?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly it was Sljivancanin who spoke. He addressed the territorials. He said the guards brigade was withdrawing from the area, that the 80th Brigade would stay there, that it would establish a command post there, and that from that point on any problems that came up would have to be solved with us. On that occasion he introduced Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujovic and perhaps some others, but I don't recall any others. I remembered those two from Ovcara. That meeting lasted for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when he introduced Stanko and Miroljub, in what capacity did he introduce them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely certain in what capacity he introduced them, but he introduced them as important people in the Territorial Defence. And I saw that they knew each other from before, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say you drew the conclusion that Sljivancanin knew these two individuals from before, what caused to you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that he called them by their names, both of them. This led me to conclude that he knew them. If you don't know someone, you can't say what his name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever meet a person who was nicknamed Kameni?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you first meet him? Was it before or after the Ovcara incident?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was after the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in what capacity did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: He came to see me in the brigade command on his own. He introduced himself; I had heard of him. He asked us for some kind of assistance in the form of food for his fighters, for the group he had around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I would like to -- I would like to deal with certain documents, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a small bundle of documents which have been prepared for my learned friends and for the Court; the registry have got them. And I would like to -- the witness, I hope, has got them. Now, might I just indicate - I hope to help the Court and my learned friends - that I will not be referring to all the documents, but I have little doubt that some of the documents, for example, tab 1 and 2, may be referred to. They are already exhibits and, consequently, there would be no prejudice, in my submission. There are nine tabs in total; they should be in both English and B/C/S. And if I may deal with tab 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I showed you this little document this morning. So can we go to tab 4, and hopefully -- now, certainly my bundle, English comes first, but it should then go on to B/C/S. For e-court, the following number, it should be Exhibit 426. The B/C/S version is 0436-8417, and there shouldn't be any difficulty in locating that. Now, Witness, have you got tab 4?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I'm hoping that the top left-hand corner will be the 23rd of November, running -- it's OG JUG, South, command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 23rd of November, village of Negoslavci. What exactly is this? Can you just tell us in general terms; I don't want to go through the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This document was issued by the command of OG South. It's addressed to the command of the 1st Military District, and it's a daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we return over to the second page, who is the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have it all on one page. It's Colonel Mile Mrksic, commander of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the English it's 2. I want to go then, please, in the English towards the very end. There are subnumbers on the left-hand side. In the English one can see number 1, 2, turning the page, there will be 3. And just three lines above the 3 I want to deal with that entry commencing, "All expert, organisational, and material [sic] support." Have you got that, Mr. Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So shall I read it out, and then I will ask you a question about it. So, "All expert, organisational, and material [sic] support was given to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade in resolving all issues with regards to taking over the responsibility in the AOR of OG South." Now, what exactly is -- or does the phrase, "... taking over responsibility..." mean here, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think these words, "... taking over responsibility..." refer to when OG South left, that it was now we who were responsible for it and we were supposed to solve all the issues in that area. And when they left, they left certain logistic and other equipment for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is already an exhibit. Can we go to tab 5, please, which is not an exhibit as yet. Tab 5 is a relatively new document dated the 29th of November. The B/C/S is 0465-2477 to 2478. The English translation is the same. I would like to go to tab 5. Have you got that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It should be a document reading, "State of combat morale in the units of the 80th Motorised Brigade and its further trend." 29th of November.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it is signed by Commander Vojnovic, namely yourself. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like then to go back to the first page, and it would be the second principal paragraph. It should read as follows so let's see if we can locate it, "Following the liberation of Vukovar, the command of the brigade..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. "Following the liberation of Vukovar the command of the brigade, functioning as the city command, was issued a task of ensuring the functioning of the military authority, ensuring the conditions for the revival and the establishment of the civilian government, judiciary, health, economy as well as preventing robbery and other types of crime." This is the 29th of November. What is meant by, "... the revival and the establishment of the civilian government, judiciary, health, economy..."? What is the purpose of this, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think the purpose of this was to have a civilian government set up and to create, as soon as possible, through it, the conditions for looking after people for starting up certain economic enterprises that had not been destroyed in the war, and as far as possible, securing the conditions for people to reside in the town, to prevent looting, crime, fights, killings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I please make application for this tab, tab 5, to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 437.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to move to tab 6. And I can deal with tab 6, I hope, fairly briefly. It, again, is a new document. It also is dated the 29th of November, and it is signed by yourself. Now, would you be kind enough, please, to turn that up, and the ERN number is 0465-2479 to 2484. So would you be kind enough, please, to go to the B/C/S version. So if you go back to tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tab 6, it should be 29th of November, the title of the document, "Regular combat report." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you be kind enough, please, to go to paragraph 2 j). Have you got that? It's a rather large paragraph. Paragraph 2 should read, "Situation in the units of the brigade," and then --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then it is subnumbered by letters, and I want to go to j). Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I want to go to the very last entry in paragraph 2 j). Starting, "Tomorrow, the 30th of November..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No -- oh, yes. Yes, now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It should read --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: If that's what you're referring to. "Tomorrow underground facilities are to be entered..." Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, my translation is slightly different. What I have got in my translation I will read out and we'll see whether there is a problem. "Tomorrow, the 30th of November, 1991, the engineering unit will bury about 400 bodies." And indeed there is reference earlier on to decaying coffins. Can I just deal about 400 bodies. Do you know where these bodies were found, located? Can you give us a picture? Was this an isolated incident of having to bury so many people or re-bury people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think all the bodies were found in one place. I think they were found all over the town and around the town. I know that Colonel Basic, from the command of the 1st Military District was carrying out this task. He asked me for assistance, and I gave him men to help; and I know that he did actually bury these bodies in a very civilised way. Each grave was marked with a cross, a number, and with the first and last name of the person if it was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would make an application that tab 6 document be entered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 438.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, can we move on to tab 7. Have you got that? It should be, "Command of the 80th Motorised Brigade." The date is the 22nd of December, and it's signed by --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, it should be the 22nd, not the 2nd. What date do you have on the original?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And it's signed by -- I think it's Lieutenant Vasic. Is that right? I know it's down as Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... called Vasic should be Lieutenant-Colonel. It's just a personal observation.
