But in relation to this particular document, can we deal, please, with the situation as such. Is this a report that around midnight on the 21st of December three members of the TO Vukovar were killed in Vukovar, there was an attempt made to cut the throat of one of them, who was later shot dead, as well as two others. That the killed men were members of the Leva Supoderica under the command of Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni. What I would like to deal with, please, is the final paragraph starting, "The scene of crime was secured..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "The scene of crime was secured by the military police and the SUP, Secretariat for Internal Affairs, and Vukovar police." Now, this is the 22nd of December. Were the military police still actively involved in investigating these sort of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to these kind of crimes, the military police helped wherever they could. I think at that time a police company had already been formed in Vukovar. This was an exceptional incident, and it was reported to the command of the 1st Military District. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: -- the neighbourhood is Hollywood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think that you said that "the neighbourhood is Hollywood," perhaps we can assume that that may not be quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct, it is. There was a neighbourhood which was a very nice one, and certain members of the TO went to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so it became known as Hollywood, or just it was Hollywood generally within the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, in any event, I would like that to be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 439, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on. We've only got two other tabs. This is tab 8. It deals with the 14th of January, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It relates again to the command of the 1st Military District, to the command of the 24th Corps, and I want to deal with paragraph 3, if I may. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that -- may I read it. "All units commenced the march to home garrisons according to plan and in an organised manner on the 14th of January, 1992." Now, does that basically mean that the 80th Motorised Brigade had finished what I will call their tour of duty and were returning to their home garrison?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Units of the 80th Motorised Brigade all returned, and the subordinate command in Vukovar only some parts of the brigade came back, which had already been working in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can certainly put that in as an exhibit, but it may well be that my learned friends will be willing to admit that the 80th Motorised Brigade returned on the 14th of January, 1992, and we can do it without a document. Now, it's entirely up to them, if -- I don't know, a slightly irregular procedure. If they're willing to make such an admission, they could say so now or we could put the document in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to state on behalf of all of the Defence teams that in view of everything that the witness said, we don't see a problem to tender this document into the evidence, in view of the fact that the -- it says that the units returned while the command stayed in Vukovar. That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 440.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, does that mean it's an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's as I understood the answer of Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then finally, may I go to tab 9? And I would like to go into private session with regard to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While my colleague Vasic is preparing himself, I would just like to make a comment just so it doesn't seem as if the Defence reacted in a way that was not appropriate to the interests of the case, and this is in regard to the proposal by the Prosecutor to agree about the document without it being admitted. At no point did the learned friend from the Prosecution, before he suggested this, he didn't tell us about this, not when he gave us this document two days ago when we talked about facts not in dispute. Maybe it's -- it's not the intention of the Defence to burden the Trial Chamber with a lot of documents, but in this particular matter I think that the Prosecutor could have asked us what we wanted to do earlier, before he made this proposal. So it seems a little bit unfair that we are being asked to respond to this suggestion in front of the Trial Chamber at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Since you and I speak the same language, I would like to ask you, for the sake of the interpreters, after I put a question to you, to wait a little bit so that the interpreters could completely translate my question and then could completely translate your answer. Thank you. You talked about your military career which spanned an imposing number of years. You told us all the functions that you occupied, and you told us about your education and training. We heard that you served at one point in your career as an officer in Slovenia. My question is if you were ever a battalion -- a commander of a battalion of the military police in your career?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never a commander of a military police battalion, but I was a commander of a military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us when were you such a commander and which unit was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was a commander of a company of the military police from 1972 until late 1976 in the 195th Infantry Brigade in the Maribor garrison in the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what was your rank at the time, and before you took up this post did you ever complete any kind of special courses or school in order to be a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was a commander of a company of the military police in the rank of a lieutenant and a captain. I finished the military police course in Pancevo in 1971, and I went for schooling in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly that from this post as a military police company you went to another post in the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to a course for battalion commanders in Sarajevo, and after that I was appointed as a deputy commander of the 2nd Infantry Battalion where I was, for less than a year, in the same unit, the same brigade that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that at one point you became a commander, I think, of the 11th Infantry Brigade in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. From October 1985 I became the commander of the 11th Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was your rank then when you were at this post and how many soldiers did the partisan brigade have, how many soldiers does any partisan brigade have?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was there in the rank of major and lieutenant-colonel, and each partisan brigade didn't have the same strength, it depended on the establishment. Mostly the strength ranged in the 2.000 number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to ask you to pause after I put my question. So perhaps you could just follow the cursor on the monitor when it jumps to the line for the answer, then you should start with your answer. Thank you. Could you please tell me -- you said in your answer to a question by my learned friend that in September 1991 you came from Slovenia to Serbia, and could you please tell me whether your unit and you personally, as its commander, had anything to do with the events in the summer of 1990 in -- in the summer of 1991 in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were blockaded in our barracks, but we -- while there we didn't do anything in terms of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell me, when you withdrew to Serbia with your unit, were you immediately assigned as commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade in Kragujevac or did you have any other duties?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. First I arrived at Gornji Milanovac and I was there for about three months, and that's at that post in that brigade which no longer existed because all of the men remained in Slovenia and the materiel and equipment were brought back. That's when I was appointed as commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were transferred and became the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, I assume that's when you met Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the post of Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was the security organ in the Kragujevac Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, all you know was that he was the security organ in the 24th Corps of Kragujevac, and the 80th Brigade belonged to that corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you received your assignment to go to the Vukovar sector, and you told us how this happened, did Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic had anything to do with this call-up of your unit and its move to carry out assignments in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him during the preparation and the organisation, but I believe that he probably was included in the work to organise and mobilise a company of the military police. Personally, as the security organ, he was not in my brigade, but I think that he was there as part of some other command in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In any case, you do have information that he was in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that he was there for a while, a short period of time, but he wasn't with me where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the 80th Motorised Brigade, after it came to the Vukovar sector, maintained contacts with its home 24th Corps in Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, generally along the -- well, we communicated through the communications system, but we didn't receive orders. I mean, it was normal for them to express an interest; I was in their unit, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that one battalion from your brigade was resubordinated to another unit in late October 1991. So could you please tell us, you as the commander probably knew which unit that was and in which sector?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That was the 1st Battalion, which was called up first, following some unsuccessful call-ups. It was commanded by Major Susa. Today he is a colonel, and a -- has a Ph.D. in military science in Belgrade. His deputy was reserve Captain Dusko Filipovic. The Chief of Staff, Rade Danilovic left with them too, he was a lieutenant-colonel, and they were resubordinated to the OG North, whose command was the command of the Novi Sad Corps and they remained as part of that composition, of their composition, until the liberation of Vukovar. Sometime until the 20th or until the end of November, until they returned to the brigade's establishment formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that after -- you said after the liberation of Vukovar. Can we agree that that was on the 18th of November, and this unit returned to your composition sometime after the 18th? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The only thing that I'm interested in a little bit, and I would like to have your expert opinion as the commander of that unit, it seems strange to me that one battalion of the motorised brigade is resubordinated to a corps, we're talking about the 12th Corps here. Isn't that something that is a bit out of the ordinary, or did this unit have some special assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It didn't have a special assignment. The resubordination of units can be done, this was done. The command of the 1st Military District army had the right to do that, and that's what it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On arrival of your unit in the Vukovar sector, can you please tell us what was the sector you occupied first. Where was your unit concentrated? You said the command was in Negoslavci. What I would like to know is where.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The command was in Negoslavci and then in the surrounding houses we had a communications company, a part of the military police company headquarters' staff, and the reconnaissance command. Then something was in -- across from the Vuka River, that was the 1st Battalion, and that was part of the Novi Sad Corps. The 2nd Battalion was in the area of Tovarnik, and the third one was at the entrance to Vukovar near the railway lines. The Howitzer battery was in the area of Negoslavci in the beginning, and then this position later changed. The mixed artillery battalion, and the armoured battalion was in the area of a cooperative, the LAD PVO, light artillery battalion, headed by (redacted) at the time, was in the area of the Sajmiste in Vukovar, one of its batteries was later subordinated to Major Stupar. The engineers' battalion in the beginning was located in Sremske Laze, even though it did come to Negoslavci itself, and in Vukovar the armoured battalion was part of the 130th Brigade, and it was in the Mirkovci sector. I don't know, I think I mentioned all the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. The military police company unit was with the brigade command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, when you received the assignment to come to the Vukovar front, am I right if I say that you or your units had the assignment of covering and taking up the occupied -- the liberated territory, as units of the second echelon, with the ultimate assignment of staying as the command of the city of Vukovar after the combat operations in Vukovar were completed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the primary task was as a reserve unit to cover the territory here, but I am sure that at the time nobody knew that it was supposed to stay in the command staff of Vukovar. When it was leaving, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you communicated with the 24th Corps, and from the reports you sent, after you remained as the commander of the town of Vukovar, I see that you were sending reports to the 24th Corps and the 1st Military District. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We were sending it primarily to the command of the 1st Military District because we were subordinated to them at the time. When we were not sending everything to the Kragujevac Corps command, sometimes we would send something to them just for their information only.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever send written regular or interim combat reports to OG South or did you sent reports to the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we cooperated with OG South. We would see them regularly. Only the 1st Military District -- you mean after the guards brigade pulled out, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When OG South existed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, only to the 1st Military District. We had nothing to do with the guards brigade then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So did I understand you properly that you never submitted any military reports to OG South, regular or interim ones?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: After they left, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said "after they left," but while OG South was in the territory of Vukovar, did you send the military reports to them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive written orders for certain tasks from the command of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you receive orders for attack in which your units would participate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you duty-bound, after receiving the written orders that you received, once the assignments were completed, to submit reports to your superior command, especially because you were a commander of a brigade where written reporting is compulsory?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for reports. We would see each other every evening and we would report back on the execution of assignments. I'm talking about OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you became the local commander of Vukovar, did you receive reports from your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. We would meet on a daily basis, we would have briefings and analyse the work in the units and the commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you didn't receive reports on regular or extraordinary events that occurred in the territory of Vukovar while you were the local commander of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But written reports on events in the Vukovar area, as long as you were the local commander there, you sent in writing to the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we sent out regular reports and reports about extraordinary events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, am I seeing it correctly that it is now time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm having some problems with the microphone. I'm trying to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let's proceed. Let's see where we left off. You said that you attended the regular briefings in the command of OG South. I would like to know whether before these briefings you first had briefings within the 80th Motorised Brigade in order to collect the information you presented to the command of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As an officer you probably know that after these regular briefings the command of the OG drew up a daily combat report which was submitted to the 1st Military District and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am not aware of that, but I think they did send those reports, because that would have been the proper thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering a question from my learned friend you said that you couldn't recall with precision, but that you thought these briefings were held from 18 to 1900 hours. If I tell you that the daily combat report of OG South was always sent at 1800 hours, do you allow for the possibility that these meetings were held before that, from 1700 hours to 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell us how one can draw up a daily combat report about the situation in the subordinated units without first receiving this information from the subordinate units at a briefing session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness has given an answer. It may not conform with the way my learned friend wishes to put his case, but all that is being asked is for the witness to speculate. He has given two specific answers, and that is the end of it, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Moore. This is cross-examination, and Mr. Vasic can ask the witness to explain, if it's necessary, how that could be done. The witness may not be able to answer at all, he may say, "I don't know." But it is not an unreasonable question. So carry on, please, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As a brigade commander you probably are familiar with the way reports are submitted, so my question was how you can explain that the commander of the OG South would be sending reports at 1800 hours to the military district about the situation in the subordinated units without first having received a report from these units and holding a regular briefing session.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Probably there was a dead-line by which an operative report had to be submitted to the command. So it's not impossible that these reports could have been written previously, as they were familiar with the situation. There were no other units there except ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the precise situation on a particular day in the zone of operations can be known only when reports arrive from all subordinated units, and you said this happened during the regular briefing sessions; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct that after being briefed the commander has the information from his subordinate units on the basis of which he can compile a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When preparing such reports, the operations officer listens to the regular briefing, and based on that he draws up a report which is signed by the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During these regular briefings was there a kind of log-book or diary into which information would be entered from these briefings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the OG there was someone whose duty it was to follow and to note down what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then, according to the rules pertaining to a brigade, this documentation, along with all the other documentation such as the operations diary, the war diary, would be kept in a special room?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a room where the conditions were right for keeping those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During these regular briefings did you come to meet Major Trifunovic, who was in the command of the OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't get to know him. Maybe I would recognise his face, but I don't know him by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that he was in the brigade command and that he worked on operations, that he was the one who kept the war diary, and therefore he probably attended these meetings, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In my brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, not in your brigade. He was from the command of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that man. I knew very few men in OG South. I've heard of his last name, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said you knew few men from OG South. I assume that you went to the regular briefings every day where, apart from officers from the brigade command, the brigade staff, the commanders of subordinate units were also present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In Operative Group South?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Only I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the commanders of the battalions or the assault detachments, the guards brigade, other units, go there? And did you all attend the regular briefings together in the command of the OG?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Only I went there from the brigade command. I saw some officers from the OG, some subordinate officers, the commanders of the assault detachment and the battalion, and they were there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Officers from the brigade command and the command of OG South were there too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Didn't you get to know most of the officers in the command of OG South and the commanders of the other subordinate units there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I stayed at those meetings very briefly, the meetings were very short, and after that we all parted ways. I did get to know some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said the meetings were short, everyone reported on what he had to say, was assigned new tasks, and returned to his unit. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After returning to your unit, if you were given a task, were so-called preparatory orders drawn up?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be kind enough to tell us when the preparatory orders were issued, what kind of tasks were those with regard to complexity or type of task?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This was done in the case of important forthcoming tasks, combat tasks. I was never given such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Exhibit 431, please. And for my learned friends, this document bears ERN number 0327-1241, 11811 in the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this document before you? It's a decision of the command of OG South dated the 16th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And would you please put page 0327-1242 on the ELMO [as interpreted], it's page 2 of this document. Thank you. Could you please zoom in to the bottom half of this page from point 8 downwards, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, in point 8 does it say that the 80th Motorised Brigade, together with a TO detachment called Stara Pazova, should take complete control over the area in the Vuka River valley, the settlement called the 6th Proletarian Division, and the Herzegovacko [phoen] Naselje neighbourhood and that part of the forces should be ready for active combat on attack axes. Is that an order you were issued by the command of OG South for your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether this is, in fact, a combat order, because the units of the 80th Motorised Brigade are ordered to take control of a certain territory and to be ready for further offensive action.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: To take control over a certain territory, yes, and not for attack, just for active operations on the attack axes. Well, yes, I see this. What I can say is that there was a Territorial Defence detachment in that part of the Vuka River valley which was not engaged in any kind of combat activity. Stara Pazova, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The part where it says, they should be ready for active combat on attack axes, that they should be ready to attack?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here, but we did not engage in any combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But the 80th Motorised Brigade is ordered, together with the Stara Pazova Territorial Defence Detachment, to carry out this order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, only the reconnaissance companies ordered to reconnoiter the area, Leva Supoderica, and to discover the presence of Ustasha forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, now you are looking at point 9; I was going to refer to that later.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is still in 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I apologise. It's under 8, 2, but I'm asking you about 8, 1, where it talks about the 80th Motorised Brigade with the Stara Pazova TO Detachment should take complete control over the territory in the Vuka River valley and should be prepared for active combat on the attack axes. This is an order addressed to the 80th Motorised Brigade together with this detachment.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To take control over this territory in the River Vuka valley. There's no dispute about that, and it was there. And should armed forces of Croatia turn up in area, they were supposed to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Item 8 doesn't mention the defence, but says to be in readiness for active operations along the axis of attack, not of defence. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there, but there was a unit there that was there to prevent any active operations in case they come in those, along those axes but that was not done because there was no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, though, that this order constitutes a combat order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, combat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember whether the OG South command, in the period from the 15th of November until the 20th of November resubordinated some other units to you which came under the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember exactly, but I know that there was a Stara Pazova Detachment and another one, that I cannot remember where it was from, that was attached to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at Exhibit 412 on the screen? And for my learned friend, the reference in English is ERN 0350-2643. Could we zoom in on the document a little bit so that Mr. Vojnovic can see it better? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is an order to which the TO Stara Pazova Detachment was resubordinated to you on the 15th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And that's the detachment which, after the 16th of November, was ordered to go into action with other units of the 80th Brigade, as we saw earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This detachment did not carry out any operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this the detachment that's mentioned in the order that we saw earlier and which, in fact, is Exhibit 431, the one that we discussed earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, this detachment did not carry out any actions throughout its time in the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I were to tell you that this detachment, which was resubordinated to you on the 15th of November, 1991, numbered about 500 men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how many men it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A detachment is a unit which is -- corresponds to a battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but it's always smaller than a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at document 372 on the monitor, please, and that is another order on resubordination of a unit to the 80th Motorised Brigade. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you see this order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the document a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this order, for the purposes of achieving as soon as possible the decisions of the 14th of November, 1991, unifying the command for forthcoming actions to be resubordinated TG 195th Motorised Brigade, 80th Motorised Brigade, for activities in the broader area of Ovcara, Jakubovac, Grabovo, and to be in readiness to mop-up the terrain in the area of the Mala Dubrava woods and the Mitnica settlement.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this tactical group never received any assignment from us to carry it out because it was part of our composition only for a day or two or two or three days. According to orders it was deployed and sent by the commander of OG South to the Grabovo sector, and that is where it remained throughout the whole time until it was no longer a part of our strength. So it was only with us for two or three days, part of our composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This tactical group, did it also number more than 500 men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many men did it have, this tactical group?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I know that this unit came from Maribor, no unit there was complete. These were mixed units, mostly anti-aircraft units, a part of the armoured battalion. So they didn't really have 200 men even.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what was part of the tactical group of the 195th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really go into their organisation now, it probably had a command, it had some units; this would be the natural composition of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you were a commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a commander of that unit; I was part of that unit. I was battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mean while the unit was in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But in Vukovar, from the 19th of November, you were the superior officer to the commander of this tactical group, Mr. Milan Jovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he came there on the 19th, he was deployed at Grabovo. I said that he had a tank company with him or maybe something more. He had an incomplete anti-artillery light battalion. He had some rear elements and the least number were the infantry forces. So it was a temporary unit which joined us, it became part of our strength. It had come from Slavonia, I don't know from which place exactly. And it left after the 20th, 21st, or the 22nd. It was no longer a part of our strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The operations group is also a temporary unit, so that is not any kind of measure.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they're not all of the same establishment composition, they don't number the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is: What level were the infantry units of this TG, which it also had a tank unit, I think you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it did. I don't think that they even had an infantry company. I don't think they even had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This unit, in accordance with this order, was engaged or it was ordered for it to go into action to secure the broader region of Ovcara, Jakubovac, and Grabovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it didn't receive that assignment from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But the execution of this task, under item 3, says that you would be issuing the orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it did not receive any orders from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this was a unit that did have sufficient forces to secure the terrain where it was sent? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Like I said, it did not receive a single order from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you if it was actually used. All I'm asking is whether it was strong enough to carry out any assignment that it was given. I wasn't asking you about whether you used it or not. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was -- it had anti-armour and anti-aircraft strength, but it had fewer infantry forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you secure a building with armoured forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the use of armoured forces, when you are supposed to defend a building attacked by infantry in a flat terrain, something that is very effective?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the terrain, the layout, the manoeuvres, the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the farm of Ovcara, it's an open area, there's nothing there except plains and the road. Would tank action against infantry, would that not be the most efficient way in a flat terrain?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You do not use tanks against infantry, you use infantry against infantry, air force against air force, and so on and so forth. Of course there could have been coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about frontal combat. I'm talking about securing or defending facilities, buildings. So did the commander of the tactical group, was he able to secure the facilities at Ovcara with his armoured -- the armoured means that he had available?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at Exhibit 420 on the monitor. And for my learned friends, this is ERN number 0327-1247. This is in the English version. We already have the B/C/S version on the screen, and now it's been zoomed in. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, you see this, an order by OG South command 446-1 of the 20th of November, 1991, at 8.00 in the morning, telling the motorised brigade, the 80th Motorised Brigade, that another unit is being resubordinated to it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is an armoured battalion of the 544th Motorised Brigade, to which you also were the superior officer following this order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In accordance with your answer earlier that the commander of the tactical group with his armoured tank company could have protected a facility, I assume that this armoured battalion could also have done that with its own armoured weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if such an assignment was issued to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But, as far as you know, none of these three units that we discussed so far that were subordinated to you from the 15th to the 20th of November, were not used to secure the Ovcara hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you something about the hangar now. You told us here, in response to a question by my learned friend, with some other senior officers you went to find this building, or this facility - am I right - where you could create a temporary or a make-shift camp for prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who were the officers that you went with to find this facility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it was a problem to find a facility. It was the only abandoned, empty facility or building, and you could not put prisoners in any other place. It was separate and it was suitable for setting up guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with this assessment. Were you familiar with this facility even before you went to look for a suitable building?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who went with you to find this building and who actually helped you if you were the one to make the decision that this building would be turned into a temporary camp for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you definitely who was with me. I don't even remember myself being there. I assume that the security organ was with me, perhaps the Chief of Staff, and someone else. Perhaps we did not decide on the facility. We were simply told to go to the building and to look it over and to see whether that can be used for our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you were ordered to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was suggested for us to go and check out this facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And since you saw the building and you consulted with your chief of security as far as the security assessment in guarding this building, and I assume you also consulted the commander of the military police company who was supposed to be in charge of the guard duty, you concluded that this was a suitable building for a collection centre for prisoners of war and other persons who had to be detained in the sector for a short period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We could not assume what it was going to be used for. We didn't know what could or what would happen, but it was a suitable building to collect military equipment and also to guard military -- prisoners of war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, this suggestion that you mentioned, was that in terms of finding a facility that could be used for equipment and prisoners or was it to find a facility which would be suitable to guard military -- prisoners of war and other persons who would be there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer? It was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The facility was not exclusively intended for prisoners of war but also for securing the equipment that was found in the area. I don't know what other purpose it was supposed to serve for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understood that the suggestion given to you was to find a facility suitable to secure prisoners of war, and that you were given this task on the 18th of November after the liberation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date when this was done or when we were given this task. I know that we did look at the facility and agree that prisoners of war could be kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a prisoner-of-war camp was actually established there on the 18th of November, 1991, and that the first group of POWs arrived there and they were secured by your units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: A group of prisoners of war arrived from Mitnica, we secured them there in accordance with the regulations and the provisions of the Geneva Convention, and we handed them over to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On that occasion you lined up all the brigade officers and some of the men and the military police company, and you appointed shifts, guards, to guard the imprisoned members of the ZNG and the MUP in the Ovcara camp - is that correct -- or this group from Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I designated the Chief of Staff as the most responsible officer on behalf of the brigade command along with a group of officers and some of the men from the military police company. I told the prisoners of war that they had to act in the way that the officers wanted in order to avoid problems, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you told the prisoners of war or, rather, their commanders that they should act in accordance with regulations to avoid problems, and you probably told them that should there be any problems, attempts to escape and so on, that guards should have the right to use fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But the commanders of these ZNG forces, which surrendered at Mitnica, took your warning seriously and there was no need to use fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The officers and the men guarding these prisoners of war were authorised to use fire-arms against anyone who would threaten the security of the facility which had been declared a temporary prisoner-of-war camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was there and he regulated all issues concerning this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I hear that they did not catch the name. That was the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Rade Danilovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understood you to say that he was authorised to decide on the use of weapons. What I'm asking is: Do the guards securing the prisoners have the right to use fire-arms in order to secure the facility and the men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, the Chief of Staff was there. He was the one in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Had it been necessary, could he have issued the order for the men to use fire-arms against the POWs, should there be a rebellion or an attempt to escape or against anyone threatening the security of the POWs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It would be up to him to assess the situation and decide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So he would have this authority?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff would have made the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that on the 18th of November, 1991, at 1800 hours you ordered around-the-clock security at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The Mitnica group, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your stay in the Vukovar area, including this period from the 18th of November, were you informed by your chief of security of the presence and the movements of two counter-intelligence groups in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would the chief of security of your unit have been duty-bound to inform you of the existence of these counter-intelligence groups, had he known about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he could have informed me, but he did not have any tasks. I did hear that there were such groups, but I don't know what their composition was or who was in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that he could have informed you; does that mean he could have but didn't have to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: If the chief of security felt there were issues about which he did not need to inform the commander, then he wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you told that in the area of Ovcara, Jakubovac, and Grabovo on the 18th, 19th, and 20th of November, there were certain security organs from the 1st Military District and from the security administration of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us -- we mention three words here very often: Ovcara, the village of Ovcara; the village of Jakubovac; the village of Grabovo. What is the distance between these villages?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Jakubovac is not a village, actually, it's a farm, raising cattle. There was an administrative building there, or two such buildings, and the distance from there to Ovcara was 1 or 2 kilometres, I don't know exactly. Grabovo was a bit further away; 3 or 4 kilometres away from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Sotin? How far was it from Jakubovac and Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I never thought about it, but it must be 7 or 8 kilometres between Sotin and Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Of course you can't know exactly, but we heard that you went to Sotin quite often to visit your units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not often, on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You went there on two occasions, on the 20th and on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the 21st, but I was there twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did this unit of yours then move somewhere else from Sotin, or did you simply stop going there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The unit remained in Sotin, it was deployed there, well-organised, doing a good job. There were no problems with that unit. I probably did go there again, but I didn't go there often. There were seven or eight battalions; I had to visit each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, it's the duty of a commander, but let me try to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see Exhibit 371 on the monitor? It's the entry for the 21st of November, 1991, at 0800 hours. For the sake of my learned friends, I'll try to find the page in English. It's page 74693 11824. Could we look at the top of the page? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You see here the 21st of November, 1991, at 0800 hours. It says: "The commander" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down a little bit? I need 8.00. Yes, yes. That's very good now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It says: "The commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade goes to Vukovar and then to the village of Sotin to visit units and on other tasks." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So I wasn't mistaken when I said you went to Sotin on the 21st. Does this jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that on the 21st of November a delegation came from Kragujevac and Arandjelovac to visit your unit, and that part of that unit was taken to Sotin to visit the unit and the other part was taken to Ovcara; you remember that? As you can see, it's on this page at 12.15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can scroll down a little bit. It's on the same page here. Could we scroll down? And a bit to the right. So that we can see the time, 12.15. Yes. Excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you see now the entry for 12.15?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It should be scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, it says a trade union delegation arrived. We'll ask for assistance. Can you see it now? Now it can be seen clearly on my monitor at least. It says: "A delegation of trade unions and other representatives from Kragujevac arrived."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No -- oh, yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: "Arandjelovac and a number of representatives visited the units in Sotin and Ovcara in an organised way, presents were handed over," and so on and so forth. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some other delegations that came as well. I know that they came from Miladinovac, and whether this was also from Arandjelovci and Kragujevci --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, it's in this log-book.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I know that on one occasion Vlado Stojanovic brought a delegation along. He was the Chief of Staff of the 1st Military District. I don't remember that they were in Sotin and Ovcara. I'm not saying they weren't, but I don't recall this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the transcript it says that this is a question, in fact we know it's an answer. Now let me ask you the following -- oh, it's been corrected now. Do you recall when General Vlado Stojanovic, the Chief of Staff of the 1st Military District, brought a delegation to see you in Negoslavci or Sotin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to the Vukovar barracks Vlado brought a delegation there. I think they were from Miladinovci. Perhaps there were people there from other towns as well. They wanted to know when the soldiers and the officers could go back to their garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume this was soon after you and your unit went to the Vukovar barracks and transferred there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how long this was after the fall of Vukovar, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in December. I am not sure about the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, then this has nothing to do with the entry we are looking at now in the operations log?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, people didn't really dare go to Vukovar. It wasn't easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But the arrival of General Vlado Stojanovic has nothing to do with this entry in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it wasn't entered. There was an officer keeping this log-book who had not been properly trained do it, and he may have left some things out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we haven't looked at that because it's not relevant. I'm asking you about the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have finished with this area of my questioning. We have only two minutes left, and it might be a better use of my time if I were to use it in order to be more efficient tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vasic. We will adjourn now for the evening. We resume tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
